- aside-browser: Read when you need a browser, or have to work across user's logged-in websites (e.g. Gmail, Slack, cloud consoles, etc.), or have to refer personal contexts like memory and browsing history.
- backend-patterns: Backend architecture patterns, API design, database optimization, and server-side best practices for Node.js, Express, and Next.js API routes.
- career-changer-translator: Translate skills from one industry to another, identify transferable skills
- coding-standards: Universal coding standards, best practices, and patterns for TypeScript, JavaScript, React, and Node.js development.
- cold-email-writer: Write personalized cold outreach emails to hiring managers and founders — specific, human, not a pitch deck
- continuous-learning-v2: Instinct-based learning system that observes sessions via hooks, creates atomic instincts with confidence scoring, and evolves them into skills/commands/agents.
- cover-letter-generator: Create personalized, compelling cover letters from resume and job description
- creative-portfolio-resume: Balance visual design with ATS compatibility for creative roles
- css-animations: CSS animation adapter patterns for HyperFrames. Use when authoring CSS keyframes, animation-delay based timing, animation-fill-mode, animation-play-state, or CSS-only motion that HyperFrames must seek deterministically during preview and rendering.
- database-migrations: Database migration best practices for schema changes, data migrations, rollbacks, and zero-downtime deployments across PostgreSQL, MySQL, and common ORMs (Prisma, Drizzle, Django, TypeORM, golang-migrate).
- demo-video: Produce a short, polished product demo video (10–40s, with composed music + sound design) for a web app, site, or feature — autonomously, end to end, and re-renderable from the repo. Use when the user says "make a demo video", "promo/teaser/launch clip", "video for Twitter/X, LinkedIn, Product Hunt, a README", "show the product working", or shares a URL and wants video. Also covers the "record the real app with Playwright" path and when to pick Remotion instead.

- docker-patterns: Docker and Docker Compose patterns for local development, container security, networking, volume strategies, and multi-service orchestration.
- e2e-testing: Playwright E2E testing patterns, Page Object Model, configuration, CI/CD integration, artifact management, and flaky test strategies.
- eval-harness: Formal evaluation framework for Claude Code sessions implementing eval-driven development (EDD) principles
- executive-resume-writer: Create C-suite and VP level resumes emphasizing strategic leadership
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- frontend-patterns: Frontend development patterns for React, Next.js, state management, performance optimization, and UI best practices.
- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.

- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing
text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's
comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including:
inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague
attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative
parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.

59	The minimal $U(1)_X$ extension of the Standard Model (SM) is a well-motivated new physics scenario, where anomaly cancellation dictates new neutral gauge boson ($Z^\prime$) couplings with the SM fermions in terms of the $U(1)_X$ charges of the new scalar fields. We investigate the SM charged fermion pair-production process for different values of these $U(1)_X$ charges at future $e^-e^+$ colliders: $e^+e^-\to f\bar f$. Apart from the standard $\gamma$ and $Z$-mediated processes, this model features additional $s$-channel (or both $s$ and $t$-channel when $f=e^-$) $Z^\prime$ exchange which interferes with the SM processes. We first estimate the bounds on the $U(1)_X$ coupling $(g^\prime)$ and the $Z^\prime$ mass $(M_{Z^\prime})$ considering the latest dilepton and dijet constraints from the heavy resonance searches at the LHC. Then using the allowed values of $g^\prime$, we study the angular distributions, forward-backward $(\mathcal{A}_{\rm{FB}})$, left-right $(\mathcal{A}_{\rm{LR}})$ and left-right forward-backward $(\mathcal{A}_{\rm{LR, FB}})$ asymmetries of the $f\bar{f}$ final states. We find that these observables can show substantial deviations from the SM results in the $U(1)_X$ model, thus providing a powerful probe of the multi-TeV $Z^\prime$ bosons at future $e^+e^-$ colliders.
60	\end{abstract}
61	
62	\vspace{-3cm}
63	\maketitle
64	
65	\section{Introduction}
66	\label{intro}
67	
68	Although the Standard Model (SM) is on a solid theoretical foundation and has been tested experimentally to great accuracy, it cannot explain the observations of nonzero neutrino masses, dark matter relic density and matter-antimatter asymmetry in the Universe~\cite{Zyla:2020zbs}. These empirical evidences and other theoretical considerations indicate the necessity for an extension of the SM. 
69	
70	
71	
72	
73	A simple beyond the SM (BSM) scenario that can in principle address some of the above-mentioned issues is to extend the SM gauge group by an additional $U(1)$ gauge symmetry. The associated neutral gauge boson (known as $Z^\prime$) has been extensively studied in the literature due to its wide range of phenomenological aspects; see 
74	
75	Refs.~\cite{Leike:1998wr,Langacker:2008yv} for reviews. 
76	 There are many ultraviolet-complete scenarios, where the $Z'$ boson naturally arises,  such as in the Left-Right symmetric models~\cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk}, and in theories of grand unification based on SO$(10)$~\cite{Georgi:1974my, Fritzsch:1974nn} and E$_6$~\cite{Gursey:1975ki,Achiman:1978vg}. The $Z^\prime$ bosons also inevitably appear in the gauge-Higgs unification scenario where the Higgs boson is identified with a part of the fifth-dimensional component of the gauge fields, and the Kaluza-Klein (KK) excited modes of the photon and $Z$ boson become $Z^\prime$ bosons~\cite{Hosotani:1983xw,Agashe:2004rs,Medina:2007hz,Hosotani:2008tx,Funatsu:2013ni,Yoon:2018vsc}. Dedicated searches for the $Z^\prime$ boson have been previously carried out at LEP~\cite{Schael:2013ita} and  Tevatron~\cite{D0:2010kuq, CDF:2011nxq}, but the most stringent bounds on the $Z^\prime$ mass and coupling currently come from the LHC dilepton searches~\cite{Aad:2019fac,CMS:2019tbu}, which also supersede the low-energy electroweak constraints~\cite{Li:2009xh}. 
77	 
78	In this paper we investigate the future $e^+e^-$ collider prospects of a general but minimal $U(1)_X$ extension of the SM where, in addition to the SM particles, three generations of right-handed neutrinos (RHNs) and a SM-singlet $U(1)_X$ Higgs field are included. The $U(1)_X$ charge assignment for the fermions in this scenario is generation-independent which makes the model free from all gauge and mixed gauge-gravitational anomalies. Reproducing the Yukawa structure of the SM, one finds that the $U(1)_X$ symmetry can be identified as the linear combination of the $U(1)_Y$ in SM and the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge groups~\cite{Appelquist:2002mw,Coriano:2014mpa,Das:2016zue,Das:2019pua}. Hence the $U(1)_X$ scenario is the generalization of the $U(1)_{B-L}$ extension of the SM~\cite{Davidson:1978pm, Marshak:1979fm}. 
79	
80	Due to the presence of the $Z^\prime$ boson with modest to large couplings to SM fermions under the gauged $U(1)_X$ extension, the model shows a variety of interesting features at the $e^+e^-$ colliders. In particular, the general charge assignment of the particles after the anomaly cancellations leads to potentially large parity violation in the fermion couplings  and distinct interference effects in the process $e^- e^+ \to f \bar f$ (where $f$ stands for the SM fermions). We investigate this process for both leptonic and hadronic final states, by analyzing the cross-sections as well as different kinematic observables, including the forward-backward asymmetry $(\mathcal{A}_{\rm{FB}})$, left-right asymmetry $(\mathcal{A}_{\rm{LR}})$ and left-right forward-backward asymmetry $(\mathcal{A}_{\rm{LR, FB}})$. We show that even if  the $Z^\prime$ boson is sufficiently heavy and off-shell (even inaccessible at the LHC), large deviations from the SM expectations in the angular distributions, forward-backward asymmetries, left-right asymmetries and left-right forward-backward asymmetries can be seen at the proposed $e^-e^+$ colliders.\footnote{Similar consequences have been predicted in the $SO(5) \times U(1) \times SU(3)$ gauge-Higgs unification formulated in the Randall-Sundrum warped space in which the KK modes of the photon, $Z$ boson, and $Z_R$ boson play the role of $Z'$ bosons \cite{Funatsu:2020haj}.} We consider various center-of-mass energy values $\sqrt{s}=250$ GeV, $500$ GeV, $1$ TeV and $3$ TeV to illustrate this effect. Furthermore, we take special care for the $e^-e^+ \to e^-e^+$ Bhabha process, which can proceed via either $s$ or $t$-channel $Z^\prime$ boson, in addition to the SM  $\gamma$ and $Z$ exchanges. Here we study the deviations in differential and total cross sections, and in left-right asymmetry from the SM results, which are then compared with the theoretically estimated statistical errors. 
81	
82	It is worth noting here that to obtain the bounds on the $Z^\prime$ boson at the LHC, the CMS and ATLAS collaborations use the so-called sequential SM where the couplings of the $Z^\prime$ boson with the fermions are exactly same as those of the SM $Z$ boson~\cite{Altarelli:1989ff}. In our $U(1)_X$ scenario, we reinterpret these bounds, properly taking into account the appropriate $Z'$ branching ratios to dileptons, and obtain the updated limits on the $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling $(g^\prime)$ as a function of the $Z'$ mass, which are then used in our numerical analysis for $e^+e^-\to f\bar{f}$.

We study different observables related to $e^-e^+\to f \overline{f}$ scattering process for $f \neq e$ in Sec.~\ref{secIII}. We discuss the Bhabha scattering in Sec.~\ref{SecV}. Some discussion on usefulness of the kinematic variables is given in Sec.~\ref{Dis}. We finally conclude the paper in Sec.~\ref{SecVII}.

131	There also exists a SM-singlet scalar $\Phi$ which generates the Majorana mass term for the RHNs after the $U(1)_X$ symmetry breaking. To introduce the fermion mass terms and the flavor mixings, the Yukawa interaction can be written as 
132	\begin{equation}
133	{\cal L}^{\rm Yukawa} = - Y_u^{\alpha \beta} \overline{q_L^\alpha} H u_R^\beta
134	                                - Y_d^{\alpha \beta} \overline{q_L^\alpha} \tilde{H} d_R^\beta
135					 - Y_e^{\alpha \beta} \overline{\ell_L^\alpha} \tilde{H} e_R^\beta
136					- Y_\nu^{\alpha \beta} \overline{\ell_L^\alpha} H N_R^\beta- Y_N^\alpha \Phi \overline{N_R^{\alpha c}} N_R^\alpha + {\rm H.c.},
137	\label{LYk}
138	\end{equation}

140	
141	
142

144

149	We see that $x_H=0$ and $x_\Phi=1$ will reproduce the $B-L$ scenario.

151	the $U(1)_Y$ and $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge groups. 
152	The $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling $g^\prime$ is a free parameter of our model which appears as either $ g^\prime x_H$ or $g^\prime x_\Phi$ in the interaction Lagrangian.

158	  \begin{align}
159	  V \ = \ -m_h^2(H^\dag H)+\lambda (H^\dag H)^2+m_\Phi^2 (\Phi^\dag \Phi)+\lambda_\Phi(\Phi^\dag \Phi)^2+\lambda^\prime (H^\dag H)(\Phi^\dag \Phi) \, .
160	  \end{align}

164	  \end{pmatrix} \, , \quad {\rm and}\quad

314	First we evaluate the LEP constraints on the model parameters for different values of $x_H$ considering $M_{Z^\prime} \gg \sqrt{s}$. Following Refs.~\cite{Eichten:1983hw, LEP:2003aa,Schael:2013ita} we parametrize the contact interactions for the process $e^+e^-\to f\bar{f}$ by an effective Lagrangian
315	\bea
316	{\cal L}_{\rm eff} \ = \ \frac{g'^2}{(1+\delta_{ef}) (\Lambda_{AB}^{f\pm})^2} \sum_{A,B=L,R}\eta_{AB}(\overline{e} \gamma^\mu P_A e)(\overline{f} \gamma_\mu P_B f) \, ,
317	\label{eq1}
318	\eea
319	where $g'^2/4\pi$ is taken to be 1 by convention, $\delta_{ef}=1\ (0)$ for $f=e$ ($f\neq e$),  $\eta_{AB}=\pm 1$ or 0, and $\Lambda_{AB}^{f\pm}$ is the scale of the contact interaction, having either constructive ($+$) or destructive ($-$) interference with the SM processes $e^+e^-\to f\bar{f}$~\cite{Kroha:1991mn}. 
320	Following Ref.~\cite{Carena:2004xs} we calculate the $Z^\prime$ exchange matrix element for our process as
321	\bea
322	\frac{g'^2}{{M_{Z^\prime}}^2-s} [\overline{e} \gamma^\mu ({x_\ell}^\prime P_L+ {x_e}^{\prime} P_R) e] [\overline{f} \gamma_\mu (x_{f_L} P_L+x_{f_R} P_R) f] \, ,
323	\label{eq2}
324	\eea
325	where ${x_\ell}^\prime$ and ${x_e}^\prime$ are the $U(1)_X$ charges of $e_L$ and $e_R$ respectively, and similarly,  $x_{f_L}$ and $x_{f_R}$ are the $U(1)_X$ charges of $f_L$ and $f_R$ respectively, all of which can be found in Table~\ref{tab2}. Matching Eqs.~\ref{eq1} and \ref{eq2} we evaluate the following bound on $M_{Z^\prime}$ as 
326	\bea
327	M_{Z^\prime}^2  \ \gtrsim \ \frac{{g^\prime}^2}{4\pi} |{x_{e_A}} x_{f_B}| (\Lambda_{AB}^{f\pm})^2 \, , 
328	\label{Lim}
329	\eea
330	considering $M_{Z^\prime}^2 \gg s$ where $\sqrt{s}=209$ GeV for LEP-II.

465	First we discuss the case of $f\neq e$ in the process $e^- e^+ \to f \overline{f}$, which only gets $s$-channel  contributions from neutral gauge bosons, i.e. $\gamma$ and $Z$ for the SM, and $\gamma$, $Z$, and $Z^\prime$ for the $U(1)_X$ model. The additional contributions in the $U(1)_X$ case will be observed from the interfere of $Z^\prime$ with the $\gamma$ and $Z$-mediated processes. In this model, quarks and leptons are differently charged under $U(1)_X$ (cf. Table~\ref{tab2}) which can be manifested in their interactions with $Z^\prime$. 
466	Similarly, the left and right-handed fermions are differently charged under $U(1)_X$ which affect their interactions with $Z^\prime$. Since the $U(1)_X$ charge and gauge coupling are assumed to be family-universal, we will consider the representative case of $f=\mu$ for leptonic final states, and $f=b$ and $t$ respectively for the down-type and up-type quark final states in  the process $e^- e^+ \to f \overline{f}$. Note that in a realistic detector environment, the top quarks can only be identified by their decay products, i.e.~bottom quarks and $W$ bosons (which are further characterized depending on whether they decay leptonically or hadronically). However, for simplicity, we restrict our study of the $Z'$ effect in the  $e^- e^+ \to f \overline{f}$ process to parton level only, which already illustrate the main points we want to emphasize, and moreover, all the numerical results presented here can be understood analytically. A full detector-level simulation, including systematic effects, detector efficiency for the leptons and misidentification of jets or leptons, is beyond the scope of the current work, and will be pursued elsewhere. Such a detailed study will be more relevant when the actual $e^+e^-$ collider is built.

478	&& \quad +8\frac{m_f^2}{s}\Big\{{\rm Re}(q^{e_R f_L} {q^{e_R f_R}}^\ast)\Big\}\Big] \, ,
479	\label{Xsec1-x1}
480	\eea

11	error-prone blocks (M$Parameters, M$ClassesDescription, M$GaugeGroups,
12	M$Information, IndexRange) so an LLM never hand-writes their Mathematica syntax,
13	and CARRY the irregular parts (Lagrangian algebra, mixing blocks, NLO
14	bookkeeping) as verbatim Mathematica strings.

17	rationals like ``-1/3``, decimals like ``1500.``, scientific ``2.5*^-3``.

32	class Rule(BaseModel):
33	    """One Mathematica replacement rule, e.g. ``CKM[1,2] -> Sin[cabi]``."""

35	    lhs: str

129	    value_rules: List[Rule] = []  # tensor Value -> { ... }
130	    complex: Optional[bool] = None  # ComplexParameter
131	    block_name: Optional[str] = None  # External only
132	    order_block: Optional[int] = None  # External SCALAR only
133	    interaction_order: Optional[Tuple[str, int]] = None  # -> {NP, 1}
134	    indices: List[str] = []  # non-empty => tensor
135	    definitions: List[Rule] = []
136	    parameter_name: Optional[str] = None
137	    tex: Optional[str] = None
138	    description: Optional[str] = None
139	    tensor_class: Optional[str] = None
140	    # tensor-only flags
141	    unitary: Optional[bool] = None
142	    hermitian: Optional[bool] = None
143	    orthogonal: Optional[bool] = None

145

147	    def is_tensor(self) -> bool:

152	        if self.is_tensor:
153	            if self.value is not None:
154	                raise ValueError(
155	                    f"parameter {self.name}: tensor uses value_rules, not scalar value"
156	                )
157	            if self.order_block is not None:
158	                raise ValueError(
159	                    f"parameter {self.name}: order_block forbidden on tensors"
160	                )
161	        exclusive = [f for f in (self.unitary, self.hermitian, self.orthogonal) if f]
162	        if len(exclusive) > 1:

164	                f"parameter {self.name}: at most one of unitary/hermitian/orthogonal"
165	            )

167	            raise ValueError(

169	            )
170	        if self.orthogonal and self.complex is True:
171	            raise ValueError(f"parameter {self.name}: orthogonal must be real")
172	        if self.parameter_type == ParamType.External and self.complex is True:

175	                "(split into real/imag or make Internal)"

180	class MassSpec(BaseModel):
181	    """Renders 0 | {sym} | {sym,val} | {sym,Internal} | {gen,{m1,v1},...}."""

183	    massless: bool = False  # -> literal 0
184	    sym: Optional[str] = None
185	    value: Optional[NumberStr] = None  # number | "Internal" | "Automatic" | None
186	    members: List[Tuple[str, Optional[NumberStr]]] = []  # multi-gen

195	class ParticleClass(BaseModel):
196	    """A M$ClassesDescription entry, e.g. ``S[100] == {...}``."""
197	
198	    spin_type: SpinType
199	    class_index: int  # the n in S[100]
200	    class_name: str
201	    self_conjugate: bool
202	    indices: List[str] = []  # -> Index[...] wrapped
203	    flavor_index: Optional[str] = None  # BARE name
204	    class_members: List[str] = []
205	    mass: Optional[MassSpec] = None
206	    width: Optional[MassSpec] = None
207	    quantum_numbers: Dict[str, NumberStr] = {}  # values are strings -> preserve -1/3
208	    pdg: Optional[Union[int, List[int]]] = None
209	    particle_name: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
210	    antiparticle_name: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
211	    full_name: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
212	    propagator_label: Optional[Union[str, List[str]]] = None
213	    propagator_type: Optional[PropType] = None
214	    propagator_arrow: Optional[PropArrow] = None
215	    unphysical: bool = False

217	    ghost: Optional[str] = None  # U[n] only
218	    goldstone: Optional[str] = None  # S[n] only
219	    weyl_components: List[str] = []
220	    majorana_phase: Optional[str] = None

228	    def _check(self) -> "ParticleClass":
229	        if self.unphysical:
230	            if self.mass or self.pdg:
231	                raise ValueError(
232	                    f"particle {self.class_name}: unphysical fields omit mass/pdg"

237	                )

239	            if not self.flavor_index:

241	                    f"particle {self.class_name}: multi-member class needs flavor_index"
242	                )

245	                self.pdg,

265	class LagrangianTerm(BaseModel):
266	    name: str  # LHS symbol
267	    expression: str  # VERBATIM Mathematica RHS
268	    delayed: bool = False  # True -> ":=", False -> "="

271	def _references(text: str, name: str) -> bool:
272	    """True if ``name`` appears in ``text`` as a whole Mathematica token."""
273	    if not text:
274	        return False
275	    return re.search(rf"(?<![A-Za-z0-9$]){re.escape(name)}(?![A-Za-z0-9$])", text) is not None
276

278	def _param_refs(p: Parameter, names: set) -> set:
279	    """Names of other parameters referenced by ``p``'s value/rules/definitions."""
280	    texts: List[str] = []
281	    if p.value:
282	        texts.append(p.value)
283	    for r in p.value_rules:
284	        texts.append(r.rhs)
285	    for r in p.definitions:
286	        texts.append(r.rhs)
287	    blob = " ".join(texts)
288	    return {n for n in names if n != p.name and _references(blob, n)}
289

291	def topo_sort_parameters(params: List[Parameter]) -> List[Parameter]:
292	    """Order parameters so each is defined before others that reference it.
293	
294	    Stable (preserves input order among independent params). Raises on a
295	    dependency cycle.
296	    """
297	    names = {p.name for p in params}
298	    deps = {p.name: _param_refs(p, names) for p in params}
299	    by_name = {p.name: p for p in params}
300	
301	    ordered: List[Parameter] = []
302	    emitted: set = set()
303	    remaining = [p.name for p in params]  # preserve input order
304	
305	    while remaining:
306	        progressed = False
307	        still: List[str] = []
308	        for n in remaining:
309	            if deps[n] <= emitted:
310	                ordered.append(by_name[n])
311	                emitted.add(n)
312	                progressed = True
313	            else:
314	                still.append(n)
315	        remaining = still
316	        if not progressed:
317	            raise ValueError(
318	                f"cyclic parameter dependency among: {sorted(remaining)}"
319	            )
320	    return ordered
321

323	class FeynRulesModel(BaseModel):
324	    """A complete FeynRules ``.fr`` model, ready to render."""
325	
326	    model_name: str
327	    info: ModelInfo
328	    interaction_order_hierarchy: List[Tuple[str, int]] = []
329	    interaction_order_limit: List[Tuple[str, int]] = []
330	    feynman_gauge: Optional[bool] = None
331	    vevs: List[Tuple[str, str]] = []  # {{Phi[..], vev}}
332	    gauge_groups: List[GaugeGroup] = []
333	    index_decls: List[IndexDecl] = []
334	    parameters: List[Parameter] = []
335	    particles: List[ParticleClass] = []
336	    gauge_xi: List[Tuple[str, str]] = []  # (V[3], "GaugeXi[W]")
337	    lagrangian_terms: List[LagrangianTerm] = []
338	    # Verbatim escape hatches for irregular constructs (FR$LoopSwitches,
339	    # Mix[...] mixing blocks, SUSY superfields, ...).
340	    raw_preamble: List[str] = []  # emitted after M$Information, before IndexRange
341	    raw_blocks: List[str] = []  # emitted just before Lagrangian terms
342	
343	    @model_validator(mode="after")
344	    def _check(self) -> "FeynRulesModel":
345	        labels = [p.class_label for p in self.particles]
346	        if len(labels) != len(set(labels)):
347	            dupes = sorted({x for x in labels if labels.count(x) > 1})
348	            raise ValueError(f"duplicate ParticleClass labels: {dupes}")
349	
350	        # Lorentz/Spin* are FeynRules built-ins. Colour/Gluon/Generation/SU2D/
351	        # SU2W are declared by SM.fr, which every BSM add-on is loaded on top of,
352	        # so they need no IndexRange in the add-on itself (matches the reference
353	        # S1_LQ_RR.fr, which uses Index[Colour] without redeclaring it). Only
354	        # genuinely new indices must be declared in index_decls.
355	        builtin = {
356	            "Lorentz", "Spin", "Spin1", "Spin2",
357	            "Colour", "Gluon", "Generation", "SU2D", "SU2W",
358	        }
359	        declared = {d.name for d in self.index_decls} | builtin
360	        used = {i for p in self.particles for i in p.indices} | {
361	            i for prm in self.parameters for i in prm.indices
362	        }
363	        missing = used - declared
364	        if missing:
365	            raise ValueError(
366	                f"indices used without an IndexRange declaration: {sorted(missing)}"
367	            )
368	
369	        self.parameters = topo_sort_parameters(self.parameters)
370	        return self

546	\label{tabASM}
547	\end{table}
548	
549	
550	From Table~\ref{tab2} and Eq.~\ref{q} it is evident that for $x_H=-2$ the couplings of $Z^\prime$ with $q_L$ and $e_L$ are zero. 
551	Therefore only the quantity $s|q^{\rm{RR}}|$ gives a resonance at $M_{Z^\prime}$, as shown in the left column of  Fig.~\ref{propagator-2}. For $x_H=-1$, there is no coupling between $e_R$ and $Z^\prime$; as a result only $s|q^{\rm{LL}}|$ contributes to the $Z'$ resonance in the $e^-e^+ \to \mu^-\mu^+$ process, as shown in the top row, second column, whereas both $s|q^{\rm{LL}}|$ and $s|q^{\rm{LR}}|$  contribute in the $b\overline{b}$ and $t \overline{t}$ cases. 
552	In case of $x_H=1$ the coupling between $d_R$ and $Z^\prime$ vanishes; therefore, the $Z'$ contributions from $s|q^{\rm{LL}}|$ and $s|q^{\rm{RL}}|$ only are observed in the $e^-e^+ \to b \overline{b}$ process. 
553	At $x_H=2$ all the $s|q^{XY}|$ quantities contribute to the $Z'$ resonance in $e^-e^+ \to f \overline{f}$ because in this case all the charged fermions have non-vanishing couplings with $Z^\prime$.\footnote{For completeness we point out that at $x_H=-0.5$, the coupling between $u_R$ and $Z^\prime$ is zero. 
554	This scenario can be observed for the process $e^-e^+ \to t \overline{t}$ where the quantities $s|q^{\rm{LL}}|$ and $s|q^{\rm{RL}}|$ only contribute to the $Z'$ resonance. } The effects of $Z'$ on the $q^{\rm XY}$ observables depending on the $x_H$ values are summarized in Table~\ref{tabASM}. 
555	
556	
557	
558	
559	\subsection{Total cross section}
560	
561	An important advantage of lepton colliders is that the incoming beams can be polarized. Let us consider the polarized electron and positron beams with the polarization fractions $P_{e^-}$ and $P_{e^+}$ respectively. 
562	The differential scattering cross section of the process $e^-e^+ \to f \overline{f}$ can be written as 
563	\bea
564	\frac{d\sigma}{d\cos\theta}(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}, \cos\theta) & \ = \ &(1-P_{e^-} P_{e^+})\frac{1}{4}\Bigg\{(1-P_{\rm{eff}}) \frac{d\sigma^{\rm{LR}}(\cos\theta)}{d\cos\theta}\nonumber \\
565	&& \qquad \qquad +(1+P_{\rm{eff}}) \frac{d\sigma^{\rm{RL}}(\cos\theta)}{d\cos\theta}\Bigg\} \, , 
566	\label{Xsec0}
567	\eea
568	where $P_{\rm{eff}}=\frac{P_{e^-}-P_{e^+}}{1-P_{e^-} P_{e^+}}$ is the effective polarization, and the differential cross sections $\frac{d\sigma^{\rm{LR}}}{d\cos\theta} $ and $\frac{d\sigma^{\rm{RL}}}{d\cos\theta}$ have been defined in Eqs.~\ref{Xsec1-x2} and \ref{Xsec1-x1} respectively. 
569	From Eq.~\ref{Xsec0} we calculate the total cross section by integrating over the scattering angle as
570	\bea
571	\sigma(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}) \ = \ \int^{\cos\theta_{\rm{max}}}_{-\cos\theta_{\rm{max}}}d\cos\theta \frac{d\sigma}{d\cos\theta}(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}, \cos\theta)  \, , 
572	\label{Xsec2}
573	\eea
574	where $\theta_{\rm{max}}$ depends upon the experiment. Theoretically using $\cos\theta_{\rm{max}}=1$ we get
575	
576	\bea
577	\sigma(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}) & \ = \ & (1-P_{e^-} P_{e^+}) \frac{1}{4} \Big[(1-P_{\rm{eff}})\sigma^{\rm{LR}}+(1+P_{\rm{eff}}) \sigma^{\rm{RL}}\Big] \, ,  \\
578	{\rm where}  \quad 
579	\sigma^{\rm{LR}}& \ = \ &
580	 \frac{\beta s}{32 \pi} \Big[\Big(2+\frac{2}{3}\beta^2\Big)({|q^{e_L f_L}|}^2+{|q^{e_L f_R}|}^2)+ 16\frac{m_f^2}{s} {\rm Re}\Big(q^{e_L f_L} {q^{e_L f_R}}^\ast\Big)\Big] \, , \nonumber\\
581	\sigma^{\rm{RL}}& \ = \ &
582	\frac{\beta s}{32 \pi} \Big[\Big(2+\frac{2}{3}\beta^2\Big)({|q^{e_R f_R}|}^2+{|q^{e_R f_L}|}^2)+16\frac{m_f^2}{s} {\rm Re}\Big(q^{e_R f_L} {q^{e_R f_R}}^\ast\Big)\Big] \, . 
583	\eea
584	Furthermore considering $m_f \ll \sqrt{s}$ we get
585	\bea
586	&& \sigma^{\rm{LR}} \ \simeq \  \frac{s}{12 \pi} \Big[{|q^{e_L f_L}|}^2+{|q^{e_L f_R}|}^2\Big] \, , \,\,\,\,\,
587	\sigma^{\rm{RL}} \ \simeq \  \frac{s}{12 \pi} \Big[{|q^{e_R f_R}|}^2+{|q^{e_R f_L}|}^2\Big]\, .
588	\eea
589	The statistical error of the cross section $\Delta\sigma^{\rm stat}\left(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}\right)$ is given by
590	\bea
591	\Delta\sigma^{\rm stat}\left(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}\right) \ = \ \frac{\sigma(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+})}{\sqrt{N}} \, , 
592	\label{Er-1}
593	\eea
594	where $N=\mathcal{L}_{\rm{int}}~\sigma\left(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}\right)$ is the total number of signal events. The deviation of the total fermion pair-production cross section can be written as 
595	\bea
596	\Delta_{\sigma}\left(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+}\right) \ = \ \frac{\sigma^{U(1)_X}}{\sigma^{\rm{SM}}}(P_{e^-}, P_{e^+})-1 \, .
597	\label{sig-dev}
598	\eea
599	
600	
601	To study the effect of beam polarization on the cross section, we consider three polarization choices for the $e^-$ and $e^+$ beams: (i) Unpolarized case with $P_e^-=0$, $P_e^+=0$; (ii) $P_e^-=+0.8$, $P_e^+=-0.3$; and (iii) $P_e^-=-0.8$, $P_e^+=+0.3$.
